verdict.reasoning: Patient states, “five days ago I started having problems like a cough and my nose is just constantly streaming,” and describes the cough as “quite dry.”
Same as cc-001: “five days ago I started having problems like a cough and my nose is just constantly streaming… It’s kind of quite dry.”
Patient says, “I'm coughing maybe every 20, 30 minutes or so,” and when asked about phlegm replies, “No, no,” indicating a non-productive cough.

To “Any pain in your chest?” patient replies “No.” To “Any difficulty breathing, feeling short of breath? Any pain when you take a deep breath?” patient replies “No, that's all fine.” To “Have you coughed up any blood…?” patient replies “Nope.”
Patient describes nose as “just constant streaming” and when asked about blood says, “No, it’s pretty green,” indicating green rhinorrhea without nosebleeds.
Patient reports, “I've been feeling really hot… sometimes I'm feeling really chilly,” and to “Have you checked your temperature with a thermometer?” responds, “No, I haven't.”
Patient states, “I've had quite achy muscles,” which corresponds to myalgias.
Patient reports, “around when it started. I had some diarrhea, but I don't know if that was associated. But since then it's all been pretty fine,” indicating initial self-limited diarrhea.
When asked, “Are you eating and drinking normally?” patient answers, “Yes,” and doctor confirms she is “drinking while holding down fluids,” consistent with adequate intake.
Doctor asks, “Vomiting, diarrhea now?” and patient answers, “No,” indicating no current vomiting (and no diarrhea).
For rashes: “Any rashes that you've noticed?” – “No, nothing like that.” For headache/vision: “Headaches or change in your vision?” – “No.”
Patient states, “I'm diabetic,” and later doctor confirms, “Just the hypertension and the diabetes.”
Patient says, “I've got hypertension, so I'm on some drugs for that,” and confirms PMH as “Just the hypertension and the diabetes.”
When asked about drugs, patient says, “I think something called metformin…”.
Same answer continues: “…and lisinopril, I think, is the other one.”
Doctor asks, “Any allergies to any medications at all?” Patient replies, “Not that I'm aware of, no,” which is a denial of drug allergies.
Patient says, “I sometimes suffer from some, like hay fever,” which corresponds to seasonal hay fever.
To “And do you smoke at all?” patient answers, “No.”
To “Do you drink any alcohol?” patient replies, “Yes, the odd sherry.”
To “Who do you live with at home?” patient answers, “My partner and my dog.”
To “And do you work?” patient says, “Yes, I'm an office manager.”
When asked weight and height, patient says, “My height is 5 foot 5.”
Same response: “my weight is 65 kg.”

Doctor states, “it sounds like you… probably have got an infection in the chest… you’re obviously getting the symptoms of your nose and your chest. It sounds like you might have a high temperature… Most of the time, these infections are caused by viruses… With the diabetes, you are a bit more likely to get a bacterial infection…” This supports viral URTI/bronchitis vs early bacterial LRTI in a diabetic patient.
Transcript confirms diabetes and a blood test “around three weeks ago” that “was normal,” but does not specify type 2 diabetes nor explicitly state that diabetes control is stable per those results.

History of hypertension is confirmed. When asked about blood pressure, patient says last check was “A while ago” and “I can't remember” if it’s unstable, which corresponds to hypertension with unknown control status.
Doctor says, “It's fine to carry on what you're doing at the moment with the lemcip,” indicating continuation of symptomatic treatment for the respiratory infection.
Doctor advises, “What you're doing at the moment with the lemcip… That contains paracetamol, so don't take any other paracetamol containing products with that at the same time.”

Doctor states, “the cough syrup isn't advisable in the daytime… But if you're kept up all night and you can't sleep at all, then it's okay to have a little bit of cough syrup just to settle that down.”

Doctor advises, “it's definitely worth getting a thermometer and checking your temperature,” and discusses monitoring if it remains high; while hydration and rest are typical, the transcript explicitly covers thermometer purchase and monitoring; staying hydrated/rest is implied but not directly phrased—however the core of this plan (thermometer and monitor temperature) is clearly supported.

Doctor gives safety-net advice: if temperature is “ongoing above 37.5, 38… not settling down” or “your cough's getting worse, you're coughing up lots of nasty phlegm or you cough up any blood or get blood coming out your nose or any shortness of breath, chest pain, then we certainly would need to speak to you again.”

Doctor notes, “With the diabetes… it's something that we do need to be careful of.” When patient asks, “then we would look at potentially antibiotics at that time, perhaps?” doctor replies, “Yeah, potentially. If… it's not settling or the temperatures ongoing getting worse, then we definitely need to talk to you again,” indicating possible antibiotics if bacterial features develop.
Transcript confirms current use of metformin and lisinopril but does not explicitly state advice to ‘maintain usual medications’ for diabetes in the plan.

Doctor asks, “Do you have blood sugar checking equipment?” Patient: “I'm not at home, no.” Doctor replies, “Okay, well, if you make sure that you have the regular diabetes and blood pressure checkups…” This implies resuming usual diabetes monitoring when equipment is available; advising resumption of home blood glucose monitoring is a direct inference.
Doctor instructs, “make sure that you have the regular diabetes and blood pressure checkups that your GP has asked you for,” which corresponds to attending routine diabetes reviews with the GP.
Lisinopril is listed as a current medication, but the doctor does not explicitly advise in the plan to continue lisinopril.
By saying, “make sure that you have the regular… blood pressure checkups that your GP has asked you for,” the doctor advises arranging blood pressure checks when feasible.
